question: Which parts of Baldr's death appear in which source?
takeaway: The familiar story of the oath, the overlooked mistletoe, and Loki guiding the blind Höðr's hand is Snorri's. The Eddic poems allude to pieces of it, and Saxo tells a different story, where Baldr and Höðr are rivals for a woman and the fatal weapon is a sword.

beats.label: All things swear not to harm him
Attempt to bring him back from Hel

weapon.note: A mistletoe shoot, slender and fair, becomes the dart.

loki.note: Only seen bound afterwards; his role in the killing is not stated.

vengeance.note: Baldr's brother, one night old, kills Höðr.

sources.name: Baldrs draumar
sources.work: Poetic Edda (eddic poem outside the Codex Regius)

dreams.note: Baldr's bad dreams send Odin riding to Hel to question a dead seeress.

weapon.note: Höðr brings 'the famed branch', not named as mistletoe.

vengeance.note: Váli, born of Rindr, will avenge him at one night old.

dreams.note: Balderus dreams that Proserpina promises him her embrace.

oath.note: No oath; his body can only be pierced by a particular sword.

weapon.note: The sword of the satyr Mimingus.

killer.note: Hotherus, a human prince and Balderus' rival for Nanna.

vengeance.note: Bous, son of Odin and Rinda, kills Hotherus.

oath.note: Frigg takes oaths from everything except the young mistletoe.

loki.note: Learns the secret in disguise and guides Höðr's hand.

hel.note: Hermóðr rides to Hel. Baldr may return if all things weep; the giantess Þökk refuses.

vengeance.note: Váli is named as the avenger elsewhere in the Edda.

question: How does the Osiris story change across nearly 2,500 years of sources?
takeaway: The Egyptian sources in this comparison preserve episodes and ritual allusions rather than Plutarch’s continuous narrative. His account, written around 100 CE, includes the chest at the banquet, the journey to Byblos and the fourteen pieces.

sources.name: Pyramid Texts (selected utterances)
sources.work: Utterances 355–357, 364, 366 and 532; S. A. B. Mercer translation (1952)

method.note: No continuous murder scene; one passage alludes to drowning (PT 364, §615d).

body.note: Nephthys gathers the limbs; Horus joins them (PT 364, §616a–617b).

conception.note: His sister receives his seed and Horus comes forth (PT 366, §632a–d).

rule.note: The deceased, identified with Osiris, commands the spirits (PT 355, §573a–b).

contest.note: Horus subdues Set and avenges his father (PT 356, §581a–582d).

sources.name: Great Hymn to Osiris (stela of Amenmose)

murder.note: The hymn does not narrate Set killing Osiris. Lichtheim notes that Egyptian texts rarely write the slaying; this episode begins with Isis already searching (between her line markers 10 and 20).

method.note: No weapon or method is described.

body.note: The hymn does not describe the body's division or burial.

search.note: Isis searches without wearying, shades him with her plumage, and makes breath with her wings (Lichtheim, between lines 10 and 20).

conception.note: She raises the weary one's inertness, receives the seed, and bears the heir (same passage).

rule.note: The praise calls him lord of eternity, and those in the Duat kiss the ground before him.

contest.note: In the hall of Geb the Ennead gives Horus his father's kingship, and he comes out crowned (Lichtheim, after line 10).

sources.name: The Contendings of Horus and Seth
sources.work: Papyrus Chester Beatty I, recto; Alan H. Gardiner translation (1931)

murder.note: Not narrated. The tale opens with the child Horus already claiming his father's office; Gardiner notes that the plot assumes Osiris's tragedy.

method.note: The papyrus does not describe how Osiris was killed.

body.note: The papyrus does not describe the body's fate.

search.note: Isis does not search for the body in this tale.

conception.note: Horus is already a child before the tribunal; his conception is not told.

rule.note: Osiris answers from the West. His second letter threatens to send messengers for the hearts of wrongdoers; Gardiner reads him as ruling the netherworld (recto 14–15).

contest.note: The Ennead says the case has already lasted eighty years. At the close they set the White Crown on Horus and give him his father's office.

sources.name: Diodorus Siculus, Library 1.21
sources.work: Library of History 1.21; C. H. Oldfather translation (1933)

method.note: The killing is reported without specifying a weapon or method (1.21.2).

body.note: Twenty-six pieces are distributed among the killers (1.21.2).

search.note: Isis recovers the remains except the genitals (1.21.5).

conception.note: Horus is already Isis’s son; his conception is not told in this chapter (1.21.3).

rule.note: Chapter 1.21 describes burial and divine honours, not rule over the dead.

contest.note: Isis avenges Osiris with Horus’s help and kills Typhon and his allies (1.21.3–4).

murder.note: Typhon and his accomplices trap Osiris (§13).

method.note: They seal him in a fitted chest at a feast and send it downriver (§13).

body.note: Typhon divides the recovered body into fourteen pieces; fish consume the genitals (§18).

search.note: Isis follows the chest to Byblos, where a tree has enclosed it (§§15–16).

conception.note: The posthumous child is named Harpocrates, distinguished here from the Horus who fights Typhon (§19).

rule.note: Osiris returns from the other world to train Horus; these sections do not describe his rule over the dead (§19).

contest.note: Horus wins battles against Typhon, and the gods uphold his legitimacy (§19).

question: How do major Ramayanas tell Sita's abduction and ordeal?
takeaway: There is no single Ramayana. Later devotional tellings protect Sita from Ravana's touch: Kamban has him carry away her cottage without touching her, and the Adhyatma and Tulsidas versions have Ravana carry off only an illusory Sita.

sources.name: Valmiki Ramayana
sources.work: Ralph T. H. Griffith, The Rámáyan of Válmíki (1870–1874)
sources.date: composed c. 5th century BCE to 3rd century CE

deer.note: Márícha becomes the golden deer, and Ráma goes to hunt him (Griffith, Book III, Canto XLIII).

abduction.note: Rávana clasps Sítá and sets her in his car (Griffith, Book III, Canto XLIX).

hanuman.note: Hanumán searches the ashoka grove and finds her there (Griffith, Book V, Cantos XIV–XV).

war.note: Rávana dies in the battle (Griffith, Book VI, Canto CX).

ordeal.note: Sítá answers the charge and is restored after the battle (Griffith, Book VI, Cantos CXVII–CXX).

banishment.note: Not in Griffith's Books I–VI, which end at the consecration (Book VI, Canto CXXX). The banishment is told in the Uttara Kanda, often printed as Book VII and widely regarded as a later addition; that book is not in the edition linked here.

sources.name: Kamba Ramayanam
sources.work: V. S. Mudaliar, condensed English version (1970)

deer.note: Maricha appears as a golden deer and Rama hunts him (Mudaliar, Aranya Kandam).

abduction.note: Remembering a curse, Ravana does not seize Sita. He digs out her hut and carries her inside it (Mudaliar, Aranya Kandam).

hanuman.note: Hanuman finds her in the ashoka grove, guarded by rakshasis (Mudaliar, Sundara Kandam).

war.note: Ravana is killed; Vibhishana is crowned, and Hanuman tells Sita (Mudaliar, Yuddha Kandam).

ordeal.note: Sita leaps into the fire. The fire-god brings her out unburnt and returns her to Rama (Mudaliar, Yuddha Kandam).

banishment.note: This six-kandam version ends at Rama's coronation and does not tell a later banishment.

sources.name: Adhyatma Ramayana
sources.work: Lala Baij Nath translation (Sacred Books of the Hindus, 1912)

deer.note: Maricha becomes a golden deer and the illusory Sita asks Rama to catch it (Baij Nath, Aranya Kanda, chapters VI–VII).

abduction.note: Rama tells Sita to leave a shadow of herself and live in the fire for a year. She does, and Ravana takes the shadow (Aranya Kanda, chapter VII, verses 1–4).

hanuman.note: Hanuman finds her under a shimshapa tree in the ashoka grove (Sundara Kanda, chapter III).

war.note: Rama's arrow tears out Ravana's heart and he falls (Yuddha Kanda, chapter XI, verses 69–75).

ordeal.note: The fire returns the Sita entrusted to it in the forest. The illusory Sita disappears (Yuddha Kanda, chapter XIII, verses 19–21).

banishment.note: Rama tells Lakshmana to leave her near Valmiki's ashram (Uttara Kanda, chapter IV, verses 55–59).

sources.name: Tulsidas, Ramcharitmanas
sources.work: F. S. Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883)

deer.note: Maricha takes a golden deer's form and Rama hunts him (Growse, Forest, doha 22).

abduction.note: Sita enters the fire and leaves an image of herself (Forest, doha 19). Ravana seats that Sita in his chariot (doha 24).

hanuman.note: Hanuman goes to the ashoka grove and sees her there (Growse, The Beautiful, after doha 7; her mourning is doha 8).

war.note: Rama shoots thirty-one shafts: one dries the nectar in Ravana's navel and the others strike off his heads and arms. The earth reels as he falls (Growse, Lanka, chhand 29).

ordeal.note: Sita enters the fire. Her shadow and the stain of disgrace are consumed, and Fire leads her back to Rama (Growse, Lanka, dohas 105–106).

banishment.note: Growse's introduction says the Sequel omits Sita's exile and tells the story of Kakabhushundi instead.

question: Did Orpheus ever succeed? How the ending changed.
takeaway: Virgil and Ovid tell of the fatal backward glance. Plato describes a phantom shown to Orpheus. Euripides alludes to the power of his music through Admetus’s wish to rescue Alcestis; that passage does not tell us whether Orpheus recovered Eurydice.

descent.note: An allusion: Admetus imagines descending with Orpheus’s musical power, rather than narrating Orpheus’s journey.

music.note: Admetus wishes he could charm the rulers below with Orpheus’s voice.

outcome.note: No outcome for Orpheus and Eurydice is stated in these lines.
The gods show him only a phantom of his wife, because he would not die for love.

end.note: He dies at the hands of women.

death.note: A snakebite as she flees Aristaeus.

outcome.note: He looks back at the edge of light and loses her.

end.note: Ciconian women tear him apart; his head floats down the Hebrus calling her name.

death.note: A snakebite while walking with the naiads; no Aristaeus.

outcome.note: He looks back, afraid she is not following.

end.note: Torn apart by maenads; his head and lyre drift to Lesbos.

condition.note: Not to turn round until he reached his own house.

question: The Mesopotamian flood, told four times
takeaway: These accounts name Ziusudra, Atrahasis, Utnapishtim and Xisouthros. They share flood and survival motifs, but damaged tablets leave gaps: a missing detail cannot always be treated as a difference between complete stories.

beats.label: Why the gods send the flood

cause.note: The noise of overcrowded humanity keeps Enlil awake.

warning.note: Enki speaks to the reed wall of his house.

sacrifice.note: The starving gods gather like flies.

fate.note: The ending sets limits on human births; the hero's own fate is not preserved.

cause.note: The explanation falls in a broken section.

warning.note: Ziusudra hears a warning addressed to a wall. The speaker’s name is not preserved in this passage.

sacrifice.note: Oxen and sheep offered after Utu appears (Segment D).

fate.note: Given life like a god and settled in Dilmun.

hero.note: Utnapishtim, telling the story to Gilgamesh.

cause.note: Not explained; afterwards Ea rebukes Enlil for punishing everyone.

warning.note: Ea speaks to the reed hut and the wall.

birds.note: A dove, a swallow, then a raven that does not return.

fate.note: Made immortal and settled far away at the mouth of the rivers.

sources.name: Berossus, Babyloniaca
sources.work: Greek history of Babylon, known from later quotations

warning.note: Kronos warns him in a dream and tells him to bury the writings at Sippar.

fate.note: Vanishes to live with the gods.

question: Inanna in Sumerian and Ishtar in Akkadian
takeaway: The Akkadian Descent of Ishtar is a shorter, later retelling. It keeps the seven gates and the rescue, but drops the choosing of Dumuzi as a substitute and the half-year arrangement that ends the Sumerian poem.

why.note: Her stated reason is the funeral rites of Gugalanna, Ereshkigal's husband.

death.note: Ereshkigal's gaze kills her; her corpse hangs on a hook.

rescue.note: Enki makes two beings from the dirt under his nails, bearing the food and water of life.

substitute.note: She gives up Dumuzi, who did not mourn her.

halfyear.note: Dumuzi and his sister Geshtinanna each spend half the year below.

sources.name: The Descent of Ishtar
sources.date: Middle and Neo-Assyrian copies, late 2nd to 7th century BCE

why.note: No reason given; she threatens to break the gate and raise the dead.

death.note: Namtar strikes her with sixty diseases.

rescue.note: Ea creates Asushunamir to charm Ereshkigal.

substitute.note: Tammuz (Dumuzi) appears only at the end, in instructions for his mourning rites.

question: Where does Persephone's story happen, and how long is she gone?
takeaway: The hymn, Ovid, and Apollodorus agree on the abduction and the pomegranate, but not on the place, the witnesses, or how much of the year Persephone spends below. The half-year many people know is Ovid's; the oldest telling says a third.

place.note: A meadow on the Nysian plain; its location is not fixed.

cause.note: Zeus has promised her to his brother; Earth grows the narcissus lure.

witness.note: Hecate hears, and Helios, who saw everything, tells Demeter.

eleusis.note: She nurses Demophon, is revealed, and founds her temple and Mysteries.

seed.note: Hades gives her a single seed in secret.

place.note: Sicily, by Lake Pergus near Henna.

cause.note: Venus has Cupid shoot Dis so love will rule the underworld too.

witness.note: The nymph Arethusa tells Ceres she saw Proserpina below; Ascalaphus reports the seeds.

famine.note: Ceres curses the land, Sicily above all.

seed.note: She eats seven seeds in a garden.

sources.name: Ovid, Fasti 4.417-620
sources.work: Latin poem on the Roman calendar

eleusis.note: Ceres heals the child Triptolemus at Eleusis.

cause.note: Hades carries her off with Zeus's help.

witness.note: The people of Hermione tell Demeter; Ascalaphus testifies about the seed.
